{{Short description|Quartic diophantine equation in 4 variables}}
The '''Jacobi–Madden equation''' is the [[Diophantine equation]]

: <math>a^4 + b^4 + c^4 + d^4 = (a + b + c + d)^4 ,</math>

proposed by the physicist Lee W. Jacobi and the mathematician Daniel J. Madden in 2008.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Jacobi, Lee W. |author2=Madden, Daniel J. |title=On <math>a^4 + b^4 + c^4 + d^4 = (a + b + c + d)^4</math> |journal=[[American Mathematical Monthly]] |year=2008 |volume=115 |issue=3 |pages=220–236 | jstor = 27642446|doi=10.1080/00029890.2008.11920519 }}</ref><ref>[http://www.physorg.com/news124726812.html Mathematicians find new solutions to an ancient puzzle<!-- Bot-generated title -->]</ref> The variables ''a'', ''b'', ''c'', and ''d'' can be any [[integer]]s, positive, negative or 0.{{efn|In fact, any nontrivial solution must include both a positive and negative value.}}  Jacobi and Madden showed that there are an infinitude of solutions of this equation with all variables non-zero.

== History ==

The Jacobi–Madden equation represents a particular case of the equation

: <math>a^4 + b^4 +c^4 +d^4 = e^4 ,</math>

first proposed in 1772 by [[Leonhard Euler]] who conjectured that four is the minimum number (greater than one) of fourth powers of non-zero integers that can sum up to another fourth power. This conjecture, now known as [[Euler's sum of powers conjecture]], was a natural generalization of the [[Fermat's Last Theorem]], the latter having been proved for the fourth power by [[Pierre de Fermat]] himself.

[[Noam Elkies]] was first to find an infinite series of solutions to Euler's equation with exactly one variable equal to zero, thus disproving Euler's sum of powers conjecture for the fourth power.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Noam Elkies |title=On ''A''<sup>4</sup> + ''B''<sup>4</sup> + ''C''<sup>4</sup> = ''D''<sup>4</sup> |journal=[[Mathematics of Computation]] |year=1988 |volume=51 |pages=825–835 |doi=10.2307/2008781 |mr=0930224 |issue=184|jstor = 2008781}}</ref>

However, until Jacobi and Madden's publication, it was not known whether there exist infinitely many solutions to Euler's equation with all variables non-zero. Only a finite number of such solutions was known.<ref>{{MathWorld |title=Diophantine Equation–4th Powers |urlname=DiophantineEquation4thPowers}}</ref><ref name="w414">Jaroslaw Wroblewski [http://www.math.uni.wroc.pl/~jwr/eslp/414.txt Database of solutions to the Euler's equation]</ref> One of these solutions, discovered by Simcha Brudno in 1964,<ref>{{cite journal |author=Simcha Brudno |title=A further example of ''A''<sup>4</sup> + ''B''<sup>4</sup> + ''C''<sup>4</sup> + ''D''<sup>4</sup> = ''E''<sup>4</sup> |journal=[[Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society]] |year=1964 |volume=60 |issue=4 |pages=1027–1028 |doi=10.1017/S0305004100038470 |mr=0166151 }}</ref> yielded a solution to the Jacobi–Madden equation:

: <math>5400^4 + 1770^4 + (-2634)^4 + 955^4 = (5400 + 1770 - 2634 + 955)^4.</math>

== Approach ==

Jacobi and Madden started with,

:<math>a^4+b^4+c^4+d^4 = (a+b+c+d)^4</math>

and the identity,

:<math>a^4+b^4+(a+b)^4 = 2(a^2+ab+b^2)^2</math>

Adding <math>(a+b)^4+(c+d)^4</math> to both sides of the equation,

:<math>a^4+b^4+(a+b)^4+c^4+d^4+(c+d)^4 = (a+b)^4+(c+d)^4+(a+b+c+d)^4</math>

it can be seen it is a special [[Pythagorean triple]],

:<math>(a^2+ab+b^2)^2+(c^2+cd+d^2)^2 = \big((a+b)^2+(a+b)(c+d)+(c+d)^2\big)^2 = \tfrac{1}{4}\big((a+b)^2+(c+d)^2+(a+b+c+d)^2\big)^2</math>

They then used Brudno's solution and a certain [[elliptic curve]] to construct an infinite series of solutions to the Jacobi–Madden equation.

== Other initial solutions ==

Jacobi and Madden noticed that a different starting value, such as
: <math>(-31764)^4 + 27385^4 + 48150^4 + 7590^4 = (-31764 + 27385 + 48150 + 7590)^4 \, </math>
found by Jaroslaw Wroblewski,<ref name="w414"/> would result in a different infinite series of solutions.<ref>Seiji Tomita, [http://www.maroon.dti.ne.jp/fermat/dioph63e.html Solutions of a^4 + b^4 + c^4 + d^4 = (a+b+c+d)^4], 2010.</ref>

In August 2015, Seiji Tomita announced two new small solutions to the Jacobi–Madden equation:<ref>Seiji Tomita, [http://www.maroon.dti.ne.jp/fermat/dioph168e.html New solutions of a^4 + b^4 + c^4 + d^4 = (a+b+c+d)^4], 2015.</ref>
: <math>1229559^4 + (-1022230)^4 + 1984340^4 + (-107110)^4 = (1229559 -1022230 + 1984340 - 107110)^4 \,,</math>
: <math>561760^4 + 1493309^4 + 3597130^4 + (-1953890)^4 = (561760 + 1493309 + 3597130 - 1953890)^4 \,,</math>
which lead to two new series of solutions constructed by the Jacobi and Madden method.
